Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Retired
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Marianne had been retired for three years when her life narrowed around the sudden death of her younger sister, Ellen, a loss that still felt, to her, as if it had happened without warning and without time to prepare. Ellen had been the family’s steady center, the person Marianne called after doctor appointments, the one she met for lunch on Thursdays, the sister who knew the names of everyone in the extended family and kept track of birthdays Marianne herself often forgot. The death happened in a way Marianne still described in fragments rather than as a whole story: a day that seemed ordinary, a phone call that was not the one she expected, the stunned realization that Ellen was gone before there had been any chance to say goodbye. In the hours that followed, Marianne moved as if she were following instructions someone else had given her. She handled details, answered questions, and tried to remain composed for her husband and adult children, but inside she felt a fierce, sickening mix of fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame that returned each time she tried to make sense of what had happened.

In the weeks after the funeral, Marianne found herself working hard at keeping busy. Retirement had once given her pleasure—time for reading, gardening, and slow mornings—but after Ellen’s death, stillness became unbearable. She filled the days with errands, organizing closets, cleaning cupboards, and finding small tasks that would carry her from one room to another so she would not have to sit with the memories that rose when there was nothing else to do. She also began avoiding other people, especially people she had socialized with before the event. Former friends from her bridge group, neighbors who used to stop by, and couples she and her husband had known for years all became difficult to face. Seeing them reminded her that life had continued for everyone else, and that she no longer knew how to enter ordinary conversation without feeling exposed. She would let calls go to voicemail, make excuses to skip gatherings, and decline invitations she once would have accepted without hesitation. Even at family events, she positioned herself near the edge of the room and left early if she could.

Marianne had come to believe that she belonged nowhere. The sense of isolation was not simply loneliness to her; it felt like a permanent distance from other people, as though the death had marked her as someone set apart in a way others could not understand. She watched friends laugh and speak lightly about plans, and she would think that their world had stayed intact while hers had split open. One thought returned with painful regularity: she should have protected others and failed. Although she knew, rationally, that she had not been able to prevent Ellen’s death, she still found herself replaying conversations and moments beforehand, searching for what she might have noticed, done, or insisted upon. That belief left her with a heavy sense of responsibility and made contact with others feel even more difficult, as if being with people reminded her of what she had not done.

Her body, meanwhile, seemed to have stayed on the night of the loss. Marianne described feeling constantly tense and ready to react to danger, with her shoulders drawn up and her muscles tight even when she was sitting quietly at home. She could not relax even when she knew she was in a safe place. At first she thought the feeling would ease with time, but months later she still found herself scanning her surroundings, startled by abrupt sounds or by the phone ringing unexpectedly. The same tension followed her into ordinary settings that had once felt comforting. At the grocery store, a crowd or a sudden announcement over the loudspeaker could make her heart pound and her body brace, not because she believed something specific was about to happen, but because she felt unable to let her guard down. At home, in the quiet of the late afternoon, she often kept moving rather than settling into a chair, because stillness gave space for the images and feelings to surface all at once.

Even now, Marianne continues to structure her days around staying occupied and away from people who knew her before the death. Her husband has noticed that she is more withdrawn, less willing to attend dinners or community events, and less able to enjoy the small routines they once shared. What finally brought her to seek help was the sense that this way of living had become the new normal, and that she was losing not only her sister but also her place in the world. She is not sure she can return to the person she was before Ellen died, but she is hoping for some way to feel less alone, less on edge, and less haunted by the belief that she failed the person she loved most.
